articles.title: Las estrellas que mecen la NBA
articles.standfirst: La liga, especialista en cuidar y potenciar su negocio, los coloca siempre en el escaparate porque son mucho más que sus estadísticas: son rostros, iconos y referentes globales
articles.summary: La liga, especialista en cuidar y potenciar su negocio, los coloca siempre en el escaparate porque son mucho más que sus estadísticas: son rostros, iconos y referentes globales
articles.body: La NBA siempre ha sabido que hay jugadores que trascienden al parquet. Estrellas capaces de convertir cada partido en un acontecimiento y que cada temporada escriben un capítulo más de su leyenda. La liga, especialista en cuidar y potenciar su negocio, los coloca siempre en el escaparate porque son mucho más que sus estadísticas: son rostros, iconos y referentes globales. Jugadores bendecidos con un talento extraordinario y un magnetismo especial que cargan sobre sus hombros con el privilegio y la responsabilidad de representar la imagen de la competición. Son, en cierto modo, la prolongación sobre la cancha de ese icónico logo que identifica al baloncesto más poderoso del planeta. Algunos llevan años dominando y ampliando su legado, como Nikola Jokic, Kevin Durant, LeBron James, Stephen Curry o Joel Embiid. Otros han irrumpido con la fuerza de quienes están llamados a marcar una época, como Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander o Anthony Edwards. También están quienes han elevado su liderazgo hasta convertirse en el corazón de sus franquicias, como Jalen Brunson, Jayson Tatum o Cade Cunningham. Y figuras cuyo peso dentro y fuera de la pista condicionan por completo el presente y el futuro de sus equipos, como Luka Doncic, Donovan Mitchell o Giannis Antetokounmpo. Un selecto grupo de superestrellas que juegan mucho más que partidos: mueven franquicias, arrastran audiencias, construyen legados y, en buena medida, mecen los designios de la NBA. Luka Doncic ya no es simplemente la gran estrella de los Lakers. Tras la marcha de LeBron James es el pilar sobre el que el equipo angelino está construyendo su presente y buena parte de su futuro. A los 27 años entra en la edad teórica de plenitud de un jugador que ya acumula seis elecciones All-NBA y que viene de conquistar su segundo título de máximo anotador en tres temporadas, con 33,48 puntos por partido. Su influencia ha llegado incluso al despacho: la franquicia atendió a su deseo de contar con un pívot de primer nivel -Walker Kessler- y se hizo un esfuerzo para mantener a su lugarteniente Austin Reaves a su lado. Pero Luka necesita convertir incontestable dominio individual en poder colectivo. En los Lakers aún no ha reproducido el impacto que tuvo en Dallas y su historial reciente de playoffs con los angelinos deja una asignatura pendiente. Aun así, su capacidad para producir puntos, rebotes y asistencias a un ritmo reservado a leyendas —es uno de los únicos tres jugadores de la historia de la NBA junto a Oscar Robertson y LeBron James que alcanzaron 15.000 puntos, 4.000 rebotes y 4.000 asistencias en sus ocho primeras temporadas— hace que cualquier proyecto de los Lakers empiece inevitablemente por él. Jalen Brunson ha pasado de ser una estrella a convertirse en el hombre que cambió la historia reciente de Nueva York. El base de 30 años lideró a los Knicks hasta su primer campeonato en más de medio siglo, acumulando además los premios de MVP de las Finales de Conferencia y de las Finales NBA. Tres años consecutivos siendo All-NBA y su capacidad para decidir partidos le han convertido en el auténtico capitán del Madison Square Garden. Su dimensión en los grandes escenarios quedó retratada con un dato descomunal: promedió 11,2 puntos en los últimos cuartos de las Finales de 2026, la mayor cifra de la historia para un base. Brunson no necesita dominar por tamaño (mide 1,88 m), lo hace por control, carácter y capacidad para decidir. Ahora llega el desafío de sostener a un campeón que se ha convertido en el objetivo de todos. La NBA ha encontrado en el pequeño gigante de Nueva York a uno de sus nuevos rostros de poder. Victor Wembanyama está acelerando el reloj de la NBA. Con apenas 22 años y 2,24 m de estatura, el francés ya ha sido All-NBA, mejor defensor de la temporada y el primer jugador que conquista de forma unánime el premio de Mejor Defensor del Año. Su combinación de altura, movilidad, tiro y capacidad para alterar partidos desde ambos lados de la pista ha convertido a San Antonio en uno de los grandes proyectos de poder de la liga. La pregunta ya no es si será una superestrella, sino hasta dónde puede llegar. Su primera experiencia en unas Finales demostró cuánto margen de crecimiento conserva. Los Spurs llegaron a dominar tramos completos de la serie, pero no pudieron proteger sus ventajas cuando los partidos entraban en territorio de máxima presión. Wemby tendrá que ganar resistencia y experiencia para que su extraordinario impacto defensivo —líder de la NBA en tapones y en DWS, el número de victorias que un jugador aporta a su equipo gracias a su rendimiento defensivo— se traduzca también en dominio absoluto en junio. El candidato a cambiar la geometría del baloncesto ya está llamando a la puerta del trono. Nikola Jokic ha convertido lo extraordinario en rutina. Por tercer año consecutivo el pívot encabezó el ranking de ESPN después de promediar un triple-doble por segunda temporada seguida, algo que únicamente había conseguido antes Russell Westbrook. Lleva seis temporadas consecutivas terminando primero o segundo en la votación del MVP y se ha instalado en una dimensión en la que cada temporada parece exigir una nueva manera de medir su dominio. El serbio no necesita velocidad ni espectacularidad para gobernar un partido: lo hace con lectura, precisión y una capacidad única para convertir cada posesión en una ventaja. La pasada temporada añadió otra barbaridad a su colección de récords: fue el primer jugador de la historia en liderar simultáneamente la NBA en rebotes y asistencias por partido. Su tiro exterior sufrió después de una lesión de rodilla, pero el verdadero desafío de Denver sigue siendo el mismo: construir alrededor de un jugador que ha convertido el juego colectivo en una extensión de su propio talento. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander ha dejado de perseguir a la generación anterior para convertirse en uno de sus protagonistas centrales. Es MVP de la NBA por segundo año consecutivo, fue campeón en la 2024-25, y entra en la nueva temporada con la posibilidad de hacer algo que no sucede desde Larry Bird: ganar tres MVP seguidos. Su baloncesto combina eficiencia, control del ritmo y una producción ofensiva que le permite dominar sin necesitar un volumen desmesurado de tiros. El base de Oklahoma City también representa el cambio de guardia de la NBA. Esta temporada puede convertirse en el tercer jugador de la historia, junto a Wilt Chamberlain y Michael Jordan, que promedia al menos 30 puntos con un 50% de acierto durante cinco campañas consecutivas. Y aunque los Thunder no pudieron repetir presencia en las Finales, su techo sigue dependiendo en buena medida de lo que suceda cuando Shai tiene a Jalen Williams sano a su lado: juntos, Oklahoma City superó a sus rivales por 15,3 puntos cada 100 posesiones. Jayson Tatum vuelve a ocupar el centro del escenario después de una temporada marcada por el tendón de Aquiles. Su regreso fue extraordinariamente productivo pese a haber disputado sólo 16 partidos de temporada regular y seis de playoffs, y ahora dispone de meses adicionales para recuperar completamente la versión que le convirtió durante cuatro años consecutivos en integrante del mejor quinteto de la NBA. En Boston, además, la salida de Jaylen Brown eleva todavía más el peso del número uno. El desafío de Tatum es enorme porque los Celtics necesitan recuperar a su gran referencia en plenitud. Antes de la lesión ya había demostrado ser mucho más que un anotador: es uno de los tres jugadores que en las dos últimas temporadas alcanzaron simultáneamente al menos 25 puntos, ocho rebotes y cinco asistencias por partido, junto a Jokic y Giannis. Si recupera ese nivel, Boston volverá a tener en sus manos una de las grandes piezas capaces de cambiar el equilibrio de la Conferencia Este. Anthony Edwards representa la explosión de una generación que ya no pide permiso para ocupar el escenario principal. Con sólo 25 años, el escolta de Minnesota alcanzó los 28,8 puntos de media, mantuvo un 40% desde el triple con enorme volumen y se consolidó como una de las grandes amenazas exteriores de la liga. Durante la ausencia de Tatum llegó incluso a asumir el reconocimiento como el mejor alero de dos vías (ataque y defensa) de la NBA. Su techo está todavía por descubrir. Edwards ya suma 10.854 puntos antes de cumplir los 25, sólo por detrás de LeBron James y Kevin Durant en la historia de la NBA. Le queda crecer como generador para sus compañeros, una faceta en la que todavía está por detrás de las grandes superestrellas que aspiran al MVP. Pero su combinación de potencia, descaro, tiro y capacidad para aparecer en los grandes escenarios ha convertido a Minnesota en un equipo cuyo presente y futuro llevan su firma. Donovan Mitchell ya no es sólo el anotador eléctrico que llegó a Cleveland procedente de Utah. A los 30 años, viene de conducir por primera vez a los Cavaliers hasta las Finales de Conferencia y acumula siete elecciones consecutivas para el All-Star. Su capacidad para crear desde el bote y utilizar su rango de tiro para congelar defensas le convierte en el motor ofensivo de un equipo del que tiran también James Harden, Evan Mobley y Jarrett Allen. Mitchell es uno de los ocho jugadores que han promediado al menos 20 puntos en cada una de las nueve últimas temporadas. Cleveland tiene talento de sobra, pero cuando llegue la hora de la verdad, buena parte de sus posibilidades pasarán por la capacidad de su escolta para recuperar la versión demoledora que mostró en anteriores playoffs, cuando llegó a promediar 30 puntos por partido. Ahora está listo para dar el salto que separa a una gran estrella de un campeón. Giannis Antetokounmpo ha cambiado de escenario, pero no de dimensión. El griego aterriza en Miami después de una última temporada en Milwaukee limitada a 36 partidos y con la exigencia de demostrar que continúa en plena madurez competitiva. Si la salud le acompaña, sigue perteneciendo al grupo extraordinariamente reducido de jugadores capaces de combinar 30 puntos, 10 rebotes y protagonismo absoluto en ataque. Su llegada convierte a los Heat en una de las grandes historias de la temporada. Miami ha apostado una enorme cantidad de activos por el que considera su nuevo eje, y Giannis aporta algo que pocos jugadores pueden ofrecer: destruir una defensa atacando el aro, dominar el rebote y condicionar el partido desde la defensa. Además, su presencia encaja en una cultura competitiva construida alrededor de Pat Riley y Erik Spoelstra. Los Heat vuelven a tener una superestrella capaz de alterar por sí sola el mapa de la Conferencia Este. Kevin Durant pertenece ya a otra categoría: la de las leyendas que siguen siendo protagonistas cuando la mayoría de sus contemporáneos hace tiempo que abandonaron el primer plano. En su primera temporada en Houston promedió 26 puntos, 5,5 rebotes y 4,8 asistencias, con un 52% en tiros de campo y un 41,3% desde el triple, números que le valieron su duodécima elección All-NBA, esta vez en el segundo quinteto. A sus 37 años, continúa siendo uno de los anotadores más eficientes de la historia. Durant, además, no llegó a Houston para ejercer de pieza decorativa. Los Rockets hicieron uno de los grandes movimientos de la NBA al incorporarle y mantienen a su alrededor un núcleo joven encabezado por Alperen Sengun y Amen Thompson. En una carrera de 20 temporadas, KD acumula dos anillos, dos MVP de las Finales, un MVP, cuatro títulos de máximo anotador y 12 elecciones All-NBA; y ha superado ya los 30.000 puntos. Houston perdió en primera ronda el pasado curso y vuelve a exigir un salto competitivo: Durant es la experiencia, el talento y el recurso ofensivo que debe intentar abrir esa puerta. Cade Cunningham ya no es una promesa: es una de las grandes estrellas que marcan el pulso de la NBA. A sus 24 años, el base de los Detroit Pistons viene de firmar una temporada de impacto mayúsculo, con su primer All-NBA en el mejor quinteto y liderando a su franquicia hasta las 60 victorias, algo que no conseguía desde hace dos décadas. Su capacidad para controlar el ritmo, castigar los emparejamientos y generar juego le ha colocado definitivamente entre la élite, después de superar lesiones y el durísimo bache de un equipo que ganó sólo 14 partidos en 2023-24. El siguiente salto de Cunningham pasa por pulir su asignatura pendiente: las pérdidas. En los últimos playoffs promedió 5,6 por partido, el registro más alto de la historia para un jugador en una serie de al menos diez encuentros. Pero buena parte de esa carga responde también a la responsabilidad que asume en unos Pistons que necesitan otro gran generador a su lado. Detroit tiene ante sí una ventana de oportunidad inmediata y el futuro de la franquicia pasa por construir alrededor de un Cunningham que ya se mueve en el territorio de las grandes estrellas de la NBA. LeBron James sigue siendo, a sus 41 años, una de las grandes figuras que marcan el pulso de la NBA. Su longevidad no tiene precedentes: la pasada temporada disputó 60 partidos y promedió 20,9 puntos, 6,1 rebotes y 7,2 asistencias, además de un 51,5% en tiros de campo. Continúa siendo capaz de generar juego, anotar y condicionar los partidos pese al paso del tiempo. Su impacto trasciende las estadísticas y se mantiene como uno de los grandes referentes de la competición. Ahora afronta un nuevo desafío en Philadelphia, donde se incorpora a unos Sixers que quieren convertir el talento de Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown y el propio LeBron en un proyecto capaz de pelear por el campeonato. Su experiencia, su capacidad para asumir responsabilidades en los momentos decisivos y su conocimiento de lo que exige una temporada larga convierten su llegada en una pieza de enorme valor para los Sixers. A los 41 años, LeBron cambia de escenario pero mantiene intacta la ambición: quiere el anillo. James Harden continúa siendo uno de los grandes generadores de juego de la NBA. La pasada temporada dividió su curso entre los Clippers y Cleveland y, tras su llegada a los Cavaliers, promedió 20,5 puntos, 4,8 rebotes y 7,7 asistencias en 26 partidos, convirtiéndose rápidamente en el principal organizador ofensivo junto a Donovan Mitchell. Su capacidad para controlar el ritmo, crear ventajas con el balón y encontrar a sus compañeros sigue siendo una de sus grandes armas. La nueva temporada le presenta ya como una pieza plenamente integrada en Cleveland y con un papel central en un equipo que alcanzó las Finales de la Conferencia Este el pasado curso. Harden y Mitchell dispondrán ahora de toda una temporada para desarrollar su conexión, mientras los Cavaliers mantienen también a Evan Mobley y Jarrett Allen y han incorporado nuevas piezas. A sus 37 años, La Barba representa experiencia, creación y capacidad para manejar los partidos: el veterano que debe poner su talento al servicio de un proyecto que busca volver a estar entre los grandes de la Conferencia Este. Stephen Curry no es sólo una de las grandes estrellas de la NBA: es uno de los jugadores que más ha transformado la forma de entender el baloncesto moderno. Su revolución desde el triple cambió las defensas, amplió los espacios y convirtió los lanzamientos de larga distancia en el centro de muchos ataques. Con cuatro anillos y dos MVP, su legado ya está entre los más importantes de la era moderna. Y, a los 38 años, sigue siendo el faro de los Warriors. La pasada temporada promedió 26,6 puntos, 3,6 rebotes y 4,7 asistencias, lo que explica que continúe siendo el eje de la identidad y las aspiraciones de su equipo. . Pero su influencia va mucho más allá del tiro. Curry ha demostrado durante años una capacidad extraordinaria para generar ventajas sin necesidad de tener el balón, moverse constantemente y obligar a las defensas a tomar decisiones lejos de la canasta. Sigue representando una amenaza capaz de cambiar un partido en cuestión de minutos. Hay estrellas que dominan una época; Curry ayudó a cambiarla. Por eso su figura trasciende a los Warriors y se ha convertido en uno de los grandes emblemas de la liga. Joel Embiid ha construido su estatus de superestrella desde un perfil único: un pívot de 2,13 metros capaz de combinar potencia física, juego al poste, lanzamiento exterior y creación con balón. Su dominio ofensivo le llevó a conquistar el MVP de 2023 y durante años le ha situado entre los jugadores más difíciles de defender de la NBA. La pasada temporada volvió a demostrar su dimensión ofensiva con 26,9 puntos, 7,7 rebotes y 3,9 asistencias por partido. Cuando está en pista, Philadelphia juega a otra cosa. Su gran interrogante ha sido precisamente la disponibilidad. Las lesiones han condicionado distintas etapas de su carrera y han limitado su continuidad en los momentos decisivos. Aun así, su techo competitivo permanece incuestionable: pocos interiores pueden producir puntos con tanta variedad de recursos y, al mismo tiempo, proteger el aro y dominar el rebote. Es el gigante alrededor del que Philadelphia ha construido su presente y uno de los rostros que explican el poder de las estrellas en la NBA actual.

articles.title: The 10 Biggest Contract Extensions in NBA History
articles.summary: It wasn't that long ago that high-end NBA players consistently went to free agency before signing max contracts, often with new teams.
articles.body:
It wasn't that long ago that high-end NBA players consistently went to free agency before signing max contracts, often with new teams.

Here, we've highlighted the 10 biggest extensions in NBA history by total value. All 10 were signed since July 2022.

To say the least, it's good to be an NBA star right now from a financial perspective.

T-9. Anthony Edwards, Minnesota Timberwolves

Extension: Five years, $244.6 million (signed through 2028-29)

Edwards signed his extension at 21, the youngest age any player featured here has signed one. His deal is fully guaranteed with no player or team options, so he's under contract through the 2028-29 season.

If he signs another max deal with the Timberwolves that begins in 2029, he could earn nearly $90 million in the final year of that contract based on current projections.

Edwards is already one of the NBA's best players. Perhaps no player is worth a salary that big, but Edwards would be on the short list of players whom you might give it to anyway and ask questions later.

Tyrese Haliburton has never been named to the All-NBA first or second teams, but it may only be a matter of time before he gets that recognition.

In his last healthy season (2024-25), he made the All-NBA third team before going on a playoff run that had him looking like a clear top-10 player. However, Haliburton then missed the entire 2025-26 season after tearing his Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 Finals.

NBA fans should hope he gets another chance in the Finals at some point in his career.

Extension: Five years, $255.2 million (signed through 2031-32)

Victor Wembanyama just signed his extension in July, but he didn't take his full max amount. He could have received roughly $50 million more if he wins MVP, Defensive Player of the Year or makes an All-NBA team in 2026-27, yet he didn't include that language in his contract.

The Spurs did offer him the full boat, according to ESPN's Michael C. Wright , but Wembanyama "ultimately chose a contract sacrifice rooted in giving him and the organization increased ability to build a sustained title contender around him."

Wemby seems strictly focused on winning NBA championships. Leaving money on the table should give the Spurs more spending power to keep them in the Western Conference's contender tier, particularly with Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper also due new deals in the next few years.

Even if he doesn't improve, Wemby is worth every penny of his extension. But the 22-year-old should only get better over the next several seasons and make this extension look like a massive bargain.

Extension: Five years, $269.1 million (signed through 2029-30)

Evan Mobley isn't considered a Tier 1 NBA star, but he's extremely valuable nonetheless.

Offensively, he's good for an efficient 18 points per game and can knock down three-pointers. Defensively, he can both protect the rim and switch onto guards on the perimeter.

One could argue he's slightly overpaid, but that doesn't change the fact that every team would love to have him. After all, he won Defensive Player of the Year and earned a spot on the All-NBA second team in 2024-25.

The next step for the 25-year-old power forward is rediscovering his three-point stroke after he shot 29.7 percent from downtown last season.

Cade Cunningham had one of the NBA's biggest offensive loads last year, but that didn't prevent him from balling out in the playoffs. He averaged 28.1 points, 7.5 assists and 5.1 rebounds per game while guiding the Detroit Pistons within one win of the Eastern Conference Finals.

Cunningham made the All-NBA third team and earned his first All-Star nod in 2024-25. Last season, he finished fifth in MVP voting and landed on the All-NBA first team.

The Pistons should look to trade for a second star who can support Cunningham offensively on the perimeter. If they get that trade right, they could be a championship contender for years to come.

T-4. Donovan Mitchell, Cleveland Cavaliers

Extension: Four years, $276.0 million (signed through 2030-21)

The average annual value of Donovan Mitchell's new four-year extension is projected to be $69.0 million, which is tied for the highest on this list.

Mitchell is certainly one of the best guards in the league. He's received seven straight All-Star nods, has finished within the top seven of MVP voting in three of the past four seasons, and landed on either the All-NBA first team or second team in each of those seasons as well.

However, it's fair to wonder whether the Cleveland Cavaliers can win a title while paying Mitchell and Mobley as much as they are. If the Cavs fall short again this season, calls to break up their core will get even louder.

T-4. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Oklahoma City Thunder

Extension: Four years, $276.0 million (signed through 2030-31)

If anyone is worth $69.0 million annually, it's Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. The two-time reigning MVP is an efficient, high-volume scorer despite routinely facing intense defensive attention.

The Thunder will have to make some tough decisions with their core in the coming years, as they can't pay everyone. They already have SGA signed to a 35 percent max, Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren on 25 percent maxes, and they just signed Cason Wallace to a five-year, $139 million rookie-scale extension.

But no matter which direction they go moving forward, the one player they can't afford to lose is Gilgeous-Alexander.

Extension: Five years, $276.1 million (signed through 2027-28)

The big question surrounding Nikola Jokić is what his next contract will look like.

Jokić is widely expected to decline his $62.8 million player option next offseason to become an unrestricted free agent. Based on current projections, he'll be eligible to sign either a five-year, $359.5 million deal with the Denver Nuggets or a four-year, $266.5 million contract with other teams.

The Nuggets will likely give Jokić however much money he wants, though they may be hesitant to pay him more than $80 million in 2031-32, his age-36 season.

Extension: Five years, $285.4 million (signed through 2028-29)

Jaylen Brown's contract has become a major talking point around the NBA this offseason.

The Boston Celtics traded Brown to the Philadelphia 76ers in July in part because they didn't believe they could build another championship team with Brown and Jayson Tatum each earning roughly 35 percent of the salary cap.

Of the two, Brown has been less efficient offensively and less impactful from a plus/minus perspective. If they felt compelled to trade one of the two, it made sense for them to keep Tatum.

However, Brown is in the midst of his prime and coming off an All-NBA second-team selection. And he plays arguably the most coveted position in the sport.

Were the C's right to trade him? Or did the 76ers swindle their division rivals? We should start to get an answer to that question this season.

Extension: Five years, $313.9 million (signed through 2029-30)

It's been a wild few years for Jayson Tatum.

He helped lead the Boston Celtics to a championship in June 2024. One month later, he signed the largest extension in NBA history.

Less than a year after that, he tore his Achilles in the playoffs.

He came back from that injury faster than expected, but he missed Game 7 of their first-round playoff series against the 76ers with knee stiffness this past spring.

If Tatum has a healthy 2026-27 campaign and returns to his pre-Achilles injury form, he should make good on his record-setting deal.

articles.title: Bold Predictions for the 2026-27 NBA Season
articles.summary: The 2026-27 NBA season is here, making this the last chance to get in some final forecasts before too much actual information forces a change of opinion.
articles.body:
The 2026-27 NBA season is here, making this the last chance to get in some final forecasts before too much actual information forces a change of opinion.

Any remaining hot takes, out-on-a-limb opinions or bold predictions need to be made official ASAP.

Here, we'll fire off a handful of last-second prognostications, hoping for a hit rate of roughly 20 percent. That's about the upper limit for accuracy when you're trafficking in bold predictions. Do any better than that, and you're probably not being bold enough.

Let's get these done before the 2026-27 season tips off.

Victor Wembanyama Will Join Bill Russell

Most Valuable Player is generally an offense-first award. Bill Russell won it in 1965 on the strength of his transformative work on D, but in the 60-plus years since, elite offensive production has typically been central to an MVP's case.

In fact, plenty of objectively shaky defenders—Nikola Jokić, James Harden, Stephen Curry, Dirk Nowitzki, Steve Nash—have had no issue winning over the years.

Kevin Garnett (2004), Tim Duncan (2002, 2003) and Giannis Antetokounmpo (2019, 2020) offer partial counterexamples, but all three were first-option scoring stars as well as elite defenders.

Victor Wembanyama is going to flip the paradigm this season. Predicting he will again be the unanimous DPOY feels too easy to be bold, but suggesting he'll win MVP while not rating as one of the best offensive players in the league would be a major development.

That's not to say Wembanyama is a slouch as a scorer. He's a great bet to exceed last year's 25.0 points per game. At the same time, last postseason showed he had a long way to go as a self-sufficient creator—suggesting he might be best used as a finisher instead.

This is a wager on Wemby taking his defensive excellence to yet another level while performing well enough on offense to get the San Antonio Spurs to a league-best win total. At that point, his MVP case will be undeniable.

The Sixers' Starting 5 Will Play Fewer than 20 Games Together

Joel Embiid looks to be in his best shape in years, but nobody should rule out the possibility of him missing three-quarters of his team's games like he did in 2024-25. If he has another 19-game campaign, this prediction will be correct automatically.

Even with (hopefully) much better health from the former MVP, we should expect substantial load management for both him and new addition LeBron James. The smart money would be on the Philadelphia 76ers staggering rest nights so they're not without both Embiid and James if they can help it.

Jaylen Brown has missed at least 10 games in each of the last seven seasons, Tyrese Maxey hasn't played more than 70 games since 2021-22 and VJ Edgecombe...well, he seems likely to replicate last year's 75 appearances. He's the exception to the rule.

Generally, Philly will be missing one or more members of its vaunted first unit. Ideally, that'll be because it's being careful and playing the long game in a season with a championship ceiling. A more troubling possibility is that Embiid can't stay on the floor or James finally succumbs to the ravages of time.

Either way, this group isn't going to suit up together for 20 or more games.

Yaxel Lendeborg Is the Warriors' Second-Best Player

Draymond Green is going to be in the Hall of Fame. Brandin Podziemski just signed a $110 million extension. Jimmy Butler and his five All-NBA nods will be back at some point.

None of them will matter more to the Golden State Warriors' success than rookie Yaxel Lendeborg.

We need to be clear that "success" is a relative term here. Golden State will be lucky to log 40 victories as it gets older and piles up injuries. That frailty is a huge part of why Lendeborg is so consequential. He's the outlier on a roster that otherwise lacks athleticism, physical force and, well...youth.

In Summer League and preseason play, Lendeborg showcased a downhill attacking game that no one else on the roster possesses. He dominated stretches of games with size and speed, presenting matchup problems and drawing attention in ways so few of Stephen Curry's teammates have over the last few seasons.

Competitive on defense, capable of knocking down threes at high volume and able to overpower every defender who can't match his size (which is most of them), Lendeborg will be key to alleviating pressure on Curry and keeping the score close whenever the 38-year-old superstar rests.

Final Record Predictions for Every NBA Team 🔮

New NBA Power Rankings on 2026-27 Opening Night

Tyrese Haliburton Will Make All-NBA Second Team

Based on a small sample of preseason action, it feels like the right time to recklessly declare that Tyrese Haliburton is so back.

Roughly 16 months removed from tearing his right Achilles in the 2025 Finals, the Indiana Pacers superstar guard looked exactly like his old self in an Oct. 13 preseason tilt against the mostly whole Oklahoma City Thunder.

Haliburton frequently drove hard to his left (which required pushing off that repaired right Achilles tendon), finished with craft, was active on defense and flung the ball all over the floor with his trademark combination of precision and flair.

It was brilliant stuff, and if you were looking for any excuse to believe that one of the last few years' most delightful and transformative offensive forces still had every ounce of magic he showed when last healthy, well...mission accomplished.

Haliburton famously pushed too hard to reach the 65-game threshold for awards consideration once before, and you'd assume the Pacers will be extremely careful with him this season. At the same time, Indy already took its gap year and must be champing at the bit to prove it belongs right back in the middle of the contender conversation.

If that means playing Haliburton for, say, 66 games, then he's going to perform at a level that proves he still belongs among the league's true elite. A third-teamer in each of his last two healthy seasons, he is going to climb even higher in a triumphant return.

The Toronto Raptors Will Have the League's Top Defense

Last year, the Toronto Raptors ranked seventh in defensive efficiency and could have climbed higher if not for frequent struggles to control the defensive glass and a penchant for putting opposing shooters on the foul line.

Even if those minor issues persist, Toronto will still have the personnel and mentality necessary to finish atop the league in defensive efficiency.

Start with Scottie Barnes, who seems to be everywhere at once. He's the only player to total at least 250 blocks and 250 steals over the last three seasons. With him around, disruption will not be a problem. Add Kawhi Leonard and his vice-grip hands. Then sprinkle in some Collin Murray-Boyles, arguably the most intriguing young defensive weapon this side of Victor Wembanyama.

Jamal Shead is a menace. Ja'Kobe Walter has a 6'10" wingspan and made leaps in screen navigation last season.

In addition to the tools required for defensive dominance, the Raptors are controlled schematically by head coach Darko Rajaković, who does not understand the concept of "too much aggression." Toronto will smother ball-handlers with full-court pressure, engage with extremely high pick-up points in the half court and generally do everything possible to speed up opponents.

The Oklahoma City Thunder, San Antonio Spurs and Detroit Pistons will all be in the mix, but Toronto is going to emerge as the NBA's most dominant defense.

Stats courtesy of NBA.com , Basketball Reference and Cleaning the Glass . Salary info via Spotrac .

Grant Hughes covers the NBA for Bleacher Report. Follow him on Bluesky and subscribe to the Hardwood Knocks podcast, where he appears with Bleacher Report's Dan Favale .

articles.title: New NBA Power Rankings on Opening Night of the 2026-27 Season
articles.summary: The long wait is over.
articles.body:
We made it through the draft, the offseason, loads of trades and free-agency moves and the preseason. And now, the 2026-27 NBA season is here.

With opening night upon us, with all the information we could glean from all of the above, it's time to once again take stock of the entire league.

Based on the same criteria that have guided us for years—team and individual numbers, recent performance (so, in this case, the preseason), championship chances and plenty of subjectivity—this is how all 30 teams stack up right now.

His shooting percentages have been ghastly in both the summer and preseason, but Los Angeles Clippers fans have to be thanking what few lucky stars they can still see for the lottery landing them Keaton Wagler before the league stripped them of five future first-round picks. The incoming rookie averaged 17.9 points and 4.2 assists, while shooting 39.7 percent from deep, as a freshman at Illinois last season.

Reason for Concern: The Past, Present and Future

Kawhi Leonard never played past the second round for L.A. The Paul George trade that helped bring Leonard to the Clippers depleted the team's trove of assets. And the NBA's salary-cap circumvention penalties cost the Clippers five more first-round picks. It could be a decade or more before fans are able to forget the painful results of the Kawhi era.

He has almost as many turnovers as assists in the preseason, and a point guard's field-goal attempts almost quadrupling his assists is a little concerning, but Darius Acuff Jr. looks like he could be an absolute blast to follow.

The Sacramento Kings aren't going to win a lot of games in the next couple years, but Acuff's heaters will ease the pain.

Reason for Concern: The Anti-Tanking Rules

Under the old draft lottery, Sacramento trading Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis would feel like a borderline lock. The Kings aren't going to be great with them, so it would've made sense to get some assets, move them along and get worse. But now, finishing with a bottom-three record gives you worse lottery odds than finishing with one of the fourth to 10th worst records.

Navigating that with a roster that's going to lose, with or without trying, will be tough.

Reason for Optimism: Better-than-Advertised Young Core

The Milwaukee Bucks almost certainly took a short-term step back when they traded Giannis Antetokounmpo, but 32 wins isn't exactly a high bar. And Tyler Herro, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Myles Turner have all been on competitive teams. Herro and Jaquez could still be developing. There's plenty of upside with Brayden Burries and Kasparas Jakučionis, too.

The Bucks could be better than expected now, with plenty of room for future improvement.

Having said that, there isn't a single sure-fire future superstar on the roster. And Milwaukee fans got used to having that with Giannis over the last decade.

Even if they hit their relative ceilings, all the players listed above feel more like complementary players than alphas.

Final Record Predictions for Every NBA Team 🔮

Reason for Optimism: The Young Backcourt

Michael Porter Jr. and Julius Randle are the players who might be able to keep the Brooklyn Nets out of the so-called "relegation zone" (where the bottom three records have worse lottery odds than the seven teams that finish ahead of them), but Mikel Brown Jr. and Egor Dëmin provide the hope for the future.

Both could be effective, high-volume three-point shooters who can also create for others. Pairing them could give Brooklyn a dynamic, unpredictable attack.

Minnesota Timberwolves coach Chris Finch recently told reporters , "We've traded moodiness for giddiness." He didn't single out Randle, instead describing Minnesota as a moody team in recent years.

For Brooklyn, the concern is whether Randle will take too many on-ball possessions away from Brown and Dëmin.

Caleb Wilson looked like a potential superstar at North Carolina, and that was based largely on his absurd vertical explosiveness. But in the Summer League and preseason, he's shown off some smooth wing skills. And as those continue to develop, he and Matas Buzelis could quickly become one of the most dynamic young forward duos in the NBA.

A lot of their early effectiveness will be determined by Josh Giddey, whose playmaking would benefit from defenses having to take his jump shot more seriously. He's had an above- average three-point percentage in each of the last two seasons, but defenders still generally play off him and try to crowd his passing lanes. If a more consistent Giddey jumper forces opponents to play him tighter, Wilson and Buzelis will get better looks around the rim.

Reason for Optimism: Stephen Curry and Yaxel Lendeborg

Even as he enters his age-38 campaign, Stephen Curry is still one of the best shows in the league. And this season, it looks like he may suddenly have a new, more dynamic point forward to play off of. Twenty-four-year-old rookie Yaxel Lendeborg looks like a seasoned vet this preseason, with averages of 23.7 points, 12.8 rebounds and 5.9 assists. And his team-first game should quickly jell with Curry's.

Reason for Concern: Injuries (or Illnesses) Galore

For those keeping track at home, Kristaps Porziņģis, Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are all out indefinitely. There are no concrete timetables for the returns of any of them. And their salaries add up to almost $90 million and over 50 percent of the salary cap. Beyond that, Curry, Al Horford and Draymond Green are 38, 40 and 36, respectively. Durability isn't a given for any of them. And if Curry has an extended absence, this season could get real ugly, real fast.

There's plenty to like about the Memphis Grizzlies' young roster, but it's also not hard to settle on one individual player. In the Summer League and preseason, the skills that have made Cameron Boozer dominant at every previous level are translating. His "lack" of athleticism was overblown, and he's averaging 24.8 points, 10.1 rebounds and 6.0 assists per 75 possessions in these exhibition games.

Reason for Concern: Ty Jerome and Zach Edey's Health

Having said that, Boozer can't lead this team to competitiveness by himself. And Zach Edey (38.5 games per season for his career) and Ty Jerome (29 games per season over the last three years) have had a hard time staying on the floor. If those two and Boozer are together, the Grizzlies are going to surprise a lot of people. If not, they could be stuck outside the play-in.

The New Orleans Pelicans are a little like the late 2010s Orlando Magic. Like Aaron Gordon, Evan Fournier and Nikola Vučević, Zion Williamson, Trey Murphy III and Dejounte Murray are solid individual players you could imagine other teams wanting, but they just don't seem to fit together. And that could lead to a couple different potential outcomes:

Either it suddenly clicks, or they finally get some assets for some of the veterans.

Reason for Concern: No Face of the Franchise

Williamson is, ostensibly, the best player and face of this team, but he's often hurt, has yet to lead them to any playoff success and seems like a perennial fixture in trade rumors.

And while there are reasons to be intrigued by Derik Queen (his passing) and Jeremiah Fears (his fearlessness), it's hard to look at any member of the young core and see a guaranteed star right now.

Keyonte George and Ace Bailey are both worthy of a little hope. Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr., though older, certainly aren't past their primes. And if they can stay healthy, they'll make the Utah Jazz far more competitive. But the biggest reason to be optimistic about this team, without question, is Darryn Peterson, a smooth-moving 2-guard with real superstar potential. If he hits his ceiling, the Jazz could be pretty special in a few years. If he's better than expected right now, they might even challenge for a play-in spot in 2027.

Reason for Concern: Markkanen and JJJ's Health

Plenty of fans and analysts are understandably excited about the raw talent on this roster and Utah's expected pivot out of the rebuild, but the latter depends a lot on Markkanen and Jackson. If either or both miss significant time, fans may have to exercise a little patience. And for their careers, Markkanen has averaged just under 55 appearances per season, while JJJ is just under 57.

The Phoenix Suns may have been a little underestimated last season, but there's no doubt that first-year coach Jordan Ott also got the absolute most out of that roster that he possibly could. He helped make them one of the hardest-playing teams in the league, something that showed up in their opponents' turnover percentage and their own offensive rebounding percentage. And though the loss of Grayson Allen and Royce O'Neale may have cost them some of that grit, Ott will surely find a way to draw more out of everyone who's left (or joined up this offseason).

Reason for Concern: Top-End Talent after Devin Booker

Trading Allen and O'Neale for Miles Bridges was, presumably, an effort to address this concern, but after close to a decade in the league, it's pretty clear that Bridges just isn't a star. And bringing him in may have done little more than reduce the team's firepower from deep. That leaves a lot of pressure on Devin Booker to lead another "try-hard" roster to an above-.500 record.

The Washington Wizards are in a situation similar to Utah's. They have a couple of good veterans in Trae Young and Anthony Davis. They have a lot of young talent all over the roster. There's plenty of upside to be developed in Alex Sarr, Tre Johnson and Kyshawn George. But no Wizard can generate quite as much optimism as AJ Dybantsa, who looks like a dynamic point forward who can do a little bit of everything at a high level.

AD has famously struggled to be available throughout his career. And if he goes down for a long stretch this season, it could be harder to get back into play-in range than previously expected. Sarr has some potential and Deandre Ayton has plenty of experience, but the former still has a lot of growing to do on offense and the latter isn't a great defensive anchor.

After making his first All-Star team in 2025-26, Deni Avdija will certainly have the ball a little less this season, but that might actually be a good thing. Playing with Ja Morant and Damian Lillard should lead to more catch-and-shoot opportunities for Avdija, which should juice his scoring efficiency a little. And when he's on the floor with Lillard, specifically, defenses won't be able to crowd Avdija's drives as aggressively.

Reason for Concern: The Point Guard Logjam

New coach Micah Nori has already said it doesn't make a ton of sense to start Lillard and Morant together. The lack of size and defense between those two could be a problem, and they're not the only point guards Nori needs to find minutes for. Jrue Holiday and Scoot Henderson will almost certainly be in the rotation too. And while two or three of the above can ostensibly play some 2, that isn't likely to alleviate the defensive concerns.

We're still workshopping duo nicknames for Cooper Flagg and Kyrie Irving, but the pairing has a catchy ring to it, and their games should flow together just as well.

Flagg is already one of the most dangerous slashers in the league, and with Kyrie back in the lineup and dragging defenders out to the three-point line, the driving lanes should be wider than any Flagg found last season.

Reason for Concern: Dereck Lively's Health

Ideally, the Dallas Mavericks' high-end duo would be a trio. And when he's healthy, Dereck Lively II is talented enough to be included. But he's only appeared in 98 games in his three seasons, and he's still recovering from a foot surgery right now.

If he can get and stay healthy, the Mavericks could push for a play-in spot. If he remains a perennial injury risk, the ceiling is certainly lower.

Reason for Optimism: Three-Point Shooting

It remains to be seen whether the Charlotte Hornets can make up for the loss of LaMelo Ball's playmaking in the aggregate, but even without some of the looks Ball created, this team should make an absurd number of threes in 2026-27. They led the league in that category last season, are bringing back Kon Knueppel, Brandon Miller and Coby White and added Naz Reid, Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen.

Reason for Concern: Lack of Shot Creation

The aforementioned loss of Ball could take more than this season to get over. His shot creation was a huge part of last season's success, and he was also second in the NBA (behind Knueppel) in total threes made. There's some untapped potential on the playmaking front from Knueppel, Miller and White, but Charlotte's offense was better with Ball on the floor in every season he played there (and it was dramatically better with him the last two years).

Jamahl Mosley did a good job of establishing a defensive culture during his time as the head coach of the Orlando Magic, but they never found a real offensive rhythm. Orlando had a below- average offensive rating in every season Mosley coached there. And while Sean Sweeney is a defensive-minded coach himself, there's a new staff in place that will overhaul the approach on the offensive end.

Over the last two seasons, Orlando is plus-9.0 points per 100 possessions when Franz Wagner, Paolo Banchero and Jalen Suggs are on the floor. The problem is that they've only logged 318 minutes as a trio in that stretch. Since the start of 2024-25, each has missed at least 46 games. The Magic may be good when they're healthy. There just isn't a ton of evidence to suggest they will be.

There's a good amount of young (or young-ish) talent still around that helped the Atlanta Hawks reach a mid-40s win total last season, but we sort of know who and what they are by now. It's the addition of a pair of championship-winning role players from the Oklahoma City Thunder that could drive this team to the next level. Neither Aaron Wiggins nor Luguentz Dort will have huge scoring roles for Atlanta, but the latter might start, and both bring tons of defensive know-how and experience.

Reason for Concern: Lack of Traditional Playmaking

Jalen Johnson's development into a bona fide point forward made it easier to trade Trae Young, but the team's offensive rating was only good (not great) when he was on the floor last season. And having a more traditional playmaker was helpful for Johnson's scoring too. Over the course of his career, he had a 59.9 true shooting percentage when sharing the floor with Young and a 56.6 true shooting percentage when playing without him. CJ McCollum, Nickeil Alexander-Walker, Dyson Daniels and maybe even Kingston Flemings can all take a little pressure off Johnson, but there aren't any dedicated, traditional playmakers in the rotation.

Reason for Optimism: The Return of Tyrese Haliburton

The last time Tyrese Haliburton was healthy and playing meaningful basketball for the Indiana Pacers, he'd hit three first-half triple-doubles and had his team leading Game 7 of the NBA Finals. It's now been well over a year since he ruptured his Achilles in that game and basketball fans (not just the ones in Indiana) should be thrilled to have him back. Haliburton is one of the best playmakers in the league, consistently and dramatically makes his teammates better and instantly makes the Pacers relevant again.

The biggest difference between these Pacers and the ones who made the Finals is Ivica Zubac now starting in Myles Turner's spot. That obviously means a lot less three-point shooting, which could make the middle of the floor a little more crowded for Haliburton's drives. Zubac is also a better rebounder, can occupy more space on the defensive end and is probably a better interior threat on offense, but there will definitely be an adjustment period.

For the most part, we've avoided established players in this space. And the Detroit Pistons do still have some intriguing young talent we could spotlight here (like Ausar Thompson). But Cade Cunningham is only 25 himself, and he just secured a first-team All-NBA nod.

Regardless of the drama that followed the Pistons (and Jalen Duren's restricted free agency) this offseason, they have one of the best young playmakers in the NBA. And even if an improved East will make it tough for Detroit to repeat last season's success, having Cunningham means it should be competitive for a while.

Reason for Concern: Lack of Three-Point Shooting

The two big deals the Pistons signed this summer were for Duren and Thompson, neither of whom shoots threes well and both of whom should start. Pair them with Cunningham, a below- average three-point shooter himself, and it starts to get real easy to imagine spacing problems for this offense.

Duncan Robinson and new additions Isaiah Joe and John Collins can help, but either or both of Thompson and Cunningham have to start knocking down long-range shots more consistently.

Over the last two seasons, Luka Dončić averaged almost 40 points and nine assists per 75 possessions when he was on the floor without LeBron James. And now, of course, all his minutes will be played without having to share the ball (and playmaking duties) with the legend. He's also heading into the season surrounded by solid shooters and finally has a rim-running big in Walker Kessler. Add Austin Reaves to all of the above, and it's easy to imagine the Los Angeles Lakers truly scoring at will.

L.A. may have a lot of 130-plus-point nights this season, but they're also going to give up that amount fairly regularly. JJ Redick has proven an effective defensive coach, but Luka and Reaves starting together is going to put a lot of pressure on Walker Kessler to clean up mistakes. And the frontcourt depth behind him, at least for the moment, is pretty thin.

Kawhi Leonard is back in a Toronto Raptors jersey. And assuming he's relatively healthy through the regular season and into the playoffs, Toronto will be a legitimate threat to represent the East in the Finals.

Leonard, Scottie Barnes and Collin Murray-Boyles give the Raptors one of the best defensive cores in the NBA.

Barnes has emerged as one of the most exciting young point forwards. And Leonard's one-on-one scoring will make the Raptors' attack far more dangerous, particularly when schemes break down at the end of games.

Reason for Concern: Three-Point Shooting

Leonard is a far more reliable shooter than the wing he's replacing (Brandon Ingram), but Toronto is still starting three players who command little to no attention outside the three-point line in Barnes, RJ Barrett and Jakob Poeltl.

In the playoffs, when defenses are more willing to ignore non-shooters, that can create some serious spacing problems.

Trading for Kevin Durant instantly oriented the Houston Rockets onto a win-now timeline, but it really shouldn't feel as urgent for them as it does for some other title contenders.

Reed Sheppard, Alperen Şengün, Jabari Smith Jr. and Amen Thompson are all 24 or younger and have star potential—or, in Şengün's case, have already reached that level.

There's enough veteran talent here to seriously threaten for a championship, but the younger players should keep them relevant beyond KD's departure or retirement.

Still, Durant's presence means Houston should want to win it all now . Pulling that off is heavily dependent on the veterans, almost all of whom have serious durability questions.

Durant has been remarkably healthy the last few years, but he is a 38-year-old forward with a torn Achilles in his history. Fred VanVleet is coming off a torn ACL.

Steven Adams has averaged 33 games per season over the last four. Bogdan Bogdanović is 34 and has appeared in 77 games in the last two seasons. And Marcus Smart hasn't played more than 62 games since 2021-22.

For years, the Cleveland Cavaliers have appeared to have things pretty well settled at both the guard and big spots. With James Harden and Donovan Mitchell in the backcourt and Evan Mobley and Jarrett Allen inside, that's still true today. But there's long been a hole, or at least a mild concern, at the 3 in the middle of that lineup. They're certainly hoping to have it this year with Peyton Watson. And if he's the player he was from December 31 through February 1, when he averaged 22.5 points and shot 46.2 percent from deep, the Cavs could represent the East in the Finals.

Reason for Concern: James Harden's Playoff History

On balance, Harden has been a productive playoff player. He's 25th all time in career postseason box plus/minus , but there's no doubt that his lows are spectacularly low. Of his 191 playoff games, Harden has had a sub-10 game score in 45 of them. And in those 45 games, he's averaged 10.9 points and 4.0 assists, while shooting 28.0 percent from the field and 18.3 percent from deep.

Reason for Optimism: Back in the Superstar Business

The Miami Heat hit their organizational peaks with some of the biggest names in the sport on their rosters. And while Jimmy Butler certainly played like a superstar during some of his playoff runs with the Heat, Giannis Antetokounmpo is closer to the profile of the likes of LeBron James, Dwyane Wade and Shaquille O'Neal. And though he may be past his own absolute peak, he's still going to put up MVP-like numbers, when available. And if he's healthy in the spring and summer, the Heat could challenge for another championship.

Miami's front office did a good job of rounding out its rotation with good shooters. In addition to holdovers Davion Mitchell and Andrew Wiggins, Klay Thompson, Tim Hardaway Jr. and Bobby Portis all have the potential to shoot 40-plus percent from deep this season. But, barring a late-career shooting breakout from Bam Adebayo or Giannis, there's a pretty serious overlap in skills (and lack of shooting) between Miami's two best players. And that could bog the offense down a bit in key moments.

The Denver Nuggets were understandably panned for much of the offseason. After an embarrassing first-round loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves, they lost Peyton Watson—the one real shot at upside on the roster—in restricted free agency.

But adding DeMar DeRozan and Marvin Bagley III and hanging onto Spencer Jones gives Denver a second unit that may finally help it survive the non-Nikola Jokić minutes.

DeRozan's one-on-one skill is the key, but Tyus Jones' steady-handed playmaking, Spencer Jones' defense, Julian Strawther's confidence as a shooter and Bagley's finishing will all help.

Jokić is one of the most reliably available superstars of his era, but at this point, Jamal Murray, Aaron Gordon and Cameron Johnson all have to be considered pretty significant injury risks.

Gordon, in particular, has struggled to shake soft tissue injuries down the stretch. And if he's compromised in the postseason, Denver's chances at a second title will be almost nonexistent.

Years ago, when much of the league was still emphasizing versatility and small-ball, the Minnesota Timberwolves zagged, traded for Rudy Gobert and made multiple conference finals playing big. Now when much of the NBA is upsizing, Minnesota unloaded Julius Randle and Naz Reid and brought in LaMelo Ball. And after seeing just a handful of preseason possessions, it's already easy to get excited about the offensive potential of the Ball-Anthony Edwards backcourt. Both are among the most effective high-volume three-point shooters in the league. Ball is one of its best creators and passers. And Edwards will be perhaps the best finisher he's ever played with.

Minnesota's starting lineup, whether the fifth spot is occupied by Jonathan Kuminga or Ayo Dosunmu, is going to be one of the best groups in the league. But the talent behind it is largely unproven. Bones Hyland and the odd man out between Kuminga and Dosunmu will have their moments, but Terrence Shannon Jr. and Joan Beringer have a lot of growing to do before they're ready to be championship-level role players.

If you could somehow measure how much pure talent a team possesses, the Philadelphia 76ers would almost certainly be near the top of the league.

Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe make up one of the most dynamic backcourts the NBA has. Joel Embiid, when healthy, can still be a devastatingly effective scorer. Jaylen Brown is coming off a season in which he averaged a career-high 28.7 points.

And LeBron James, even in his age-42 season, can bring playmaking and know-how that ties it all together.

Health is a key consideration for plenty of teams around the league, but it's especially concerning for the Sixers.

Again, LeBron is about to turn 42. Embiid's struggles to stay on the floor have been discussed ad nauseam, and he lacked explosiveness at times in the preseason. If either or both are hurt in the playoffs, Philly's shot at a title will be at risk.

Reason for Optimism: The Potential Jaylen Brown Replacement(s)

Practically speaking, a healthy Jayson Tatum is the Boston Celtics' replacement for the 2025-26 version of Jaylen Brown. But for the Celtics to get back to championship level, they'll need someone to replace the pre-2025-26 version of Brown.

Actually, with the current roster, it'll probably have to be multiple someones. And with Paul George, Hugo González and Baylor Scheierman, Boston may be able to make up the production in the aggregate.

The Celtics have enough depth and are coached well enough to survive some absences in the regular season, but Tatum is coming off a ruptured Achilles, Paul George is oft-injured and 36 and Mitchell Robinson has his own troubles staying on the floor.

If one or more are gone in the playoffs, getting back to the mountaintop may be impossible.

Reason for Optimism: The Starters are Back

Over the course of the 2026 playoffs, the New York Knicks proved themselves to have one of the NBA's best starting lineups—if not the best.

Jalen Brunson's playmaking (for himself and others), Mikal Bridges and OG Anunoby's three-and-D contributions, Karl-Anthony Towns' shooting and rebounding, and Josh Hart's ability to fill in the gaps took New York all the way to a title.

The Knicks played most of the postseason with a seven- or eight-man rotation. Jordan Clarkson and Jose Alvarado appeared in most of the games, but they were both around 10 minutes per.

And over the offseason, they lost crucial offensive rebounder and big man Mitchell Robinson. Andre Drummond can replace some of what went out the door, but this team's depth will be tested in the 2027 postseason.

Reason for Optimism: This Is Just Getting Started

We've gotten over our skis on a number of young cores in recent years, but it's hard to imagine how this one can actually go wrong.

Victor Wembanyama, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper are 22, 21 and 20, respectively. Wemby's already a "best in the world" contender. Castle had a fringe-of-the-fringes All-Star case last season. And Harper looked like the second-best Spur for prolonged stretches of the playoffs.

All three are several years away from their primes.

For a player with Wemby's slender, 7'4" frame, health is always going to be the primary concern. And to date, he's only averaged 60.3 appearances per year. He, of course, stayed upright during last year's Finals run, but if he's hurt down the stretch, San Antonio's title chances will be shot.

Reason for Optimism: The Mid-First-Round Picks

As if the Oklahoma City Thunder needed this kind of help, it looks like they may have landed a pair of keepers in the middle of the first round this past summer.

In just 23.3 minutes, Aday Mara averaged 13.4 points, 7.6 rebounds and 2.8 assists, while shooting 78.8 percent from the field. And Bennett Stirtz added 14.6 points and 3.0 assists in 27.2 minutes, while shooting 48.4 percent from deep.

He could realistically be a concern for every team in the NBA, but Victor Wembanyama is especially tough for the Thunder. He appears to have Chet Holmgren's number in a way that legitimately shakes OKC's young star. And his dominance over him predates their time in the NBA.

If the Thunder and San Antonio Spurs meet in the postseason again, Holmgren is going to have to discover a new approach to the matchup.

articles.title: Forget Knicks and 76ers, Michelle Beadle boldly picks her 2027 Eastern Conference Finals winner
articles.summary: NBA analyst Michelle Beadle has a surprise pick for the winners of the 2027 Eastern Conference Finals. With the 2026-27 NBA season kicking off soon, experts...
articles.body:
NBA analyst Michelle Beadle has a surprise pick for the winners of the 2027 Eastern Conference Finals.

With the 2026-27 NBA season kicking off soon, experts have started releasing their favourites for the new campaign.

This includes predicting which teams will play in the 2027 NBA Finals from the Western and Eastern Conferences.

Speaking of the East, most think that the New York Knicks or the Philadelphia 76ers have the best shot at reaching the NBA Finals, but former ESPN star Michelle Beadle seems to have other thoughts.

Michelle Beadle predicts the Indiana Pacers will reach the 2027 NBA Finals

During a recent episode of the Run It Back podcast, Beadle shared her pick with co-hosts Lou Williams, DeMarcus Cousins, and Chandler Parsons.

"Alright, this is my hot take… I believe the Indiana Pacers will be representing the Eastern Conference in the NBA Finals," Beadle stated.

Of course, with the return of Tyrese Haliburton, the Pacers are expected to be among the top teams in the conference.

Moreover, the Pacers did make the 2025 NBA Finals, where they lost to the Oklahoma City Thunder. Beadle sees the Pacers repeating the same level of success next season.

But it's tough to see Beadle's 'hot take' become a reality, especially with the presence of heavy-hitters like the Knicks and the 76ers.

articles.title: Valkyries and Dream focus on defense, but why can’t WNBA Finals produce more scoring?
articles.summary: SAN FRANCISCO — Two games into the WNBA Finals, the main question on everyone’s mind has to be: Why is it so hard for these two teams to score? Game 2 ended...
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — Two games into the WNBA Finals, the main question on everyone's mind has to be: Why is it so hard for these two teams to score?

Game 2 ended with the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries making 33.9 and 34.4 percent of their field goals, respectively. The teams both shot below 33 percent from the field in Game 1. The Valkyries scraped out a win in the opener with 68 points while Dream won Game 2 with 79, which was the average points per game for the lowest-scoring team (Connecticut) in 2026. Per data from Her Hoop Stats, only two teams had won a WNBA Finals game prior to 2026 shooting under 34 percent from the field. Now, four teams have.

The basketball gods seemed to be toying with the two teams on multiple occasions, like when Rhyne Howard had a 3-pointer bounce on the rim multiple times before spilling out or when Gabby Williams threw up a wedgie. This was karmically bad.

There's no denying that these are two excellent defenses. Golden State entered with the WNBA's best defensive rating during the regular season — and the best relative to league average in WNBA history — while Atlanta was third in defensive rating. But that doesn't come close to explaining why it has been such a struggle for both teams to shoot the ball. This was a regular season that set the league record for highest field-goal percentage.

Long-distance shooters can't find their touch from 3-point range. Some of the league's best drivers are blowing their finishes inside. Everyone is missing from everywhere.

"Oh, I mean, I don't have the answer to that," Dream coach Karl Smesko said after his team's 79-65 victory.

To be clear, neither team is sweating its shooting percentages. The Valkyries pride themselves on defense; it's their identity. Before Monday's game, coach Natalie Nakase didn't know what Golden State shot from 3-point range in its previous contest, only that its defensive effort was what it needed to be in the second half.

And that defense takes a lot out of the Valkyries. They play hard all the time. The physical toll of getting into the bodies of opposing players, shifting into passing lanes, walling off drives and boxing out naturally leaves a little less in the tank for the offensive end.

Golden State also denies itself the easiest scoring opportunities because it doesn't play with much pace. The best time to score is before the defense sets, yet the Valkyries don't run the floor, preferring instead to suck the life out of the shot clock and slow the opposition. It's a winning strategy, but it did result in the Valkyries having the lowest field-goal percentage (42.2) in the WNBA in 2026 (along with the fact that they take such a high volume of their shots from 3-point range).

When Golden State tried to run in Game 2, it went disastrously. The Valkyries committed five turnovers in transition, spoiling excellent defensive possessions by being careless with the ball. The only part of the offense that Nakase was concerned with in defeat was ball control.

"(The Dream) really started to shift into those driving lanes," Nakase said. "They're there early, right, trying to create more passes for us. And so, when we're not in the right spots in terms of being able to receive those passes and see the next layer of driving lanes, then that's where it got a little bit sticky."

Scoring is also a little bit harder when your best player isn't at her best. Despite a heroic 26 points in the Game 1 win, Williams appeared to be limping down the stretch after a collision with Jordin Canada at the foul line. She had a harder time finding the bottom of the net Monday, finishing 3 of 15 from the field, though she and Nakase both denied that there was anything wrong with the Valkyries' highest-usage player.

Atlanta's struggles from the floor are a little more predictable. During the regular season, the Dream's shooting percentages against the Valkyries were: 39.4, 34.3 and 39.1 (while Golden State shot at least 43.5 percent in all three matchups). The Valkyries' defense has been difficult for Atlanta to pierce for five games now.

It starts on the interior, where the Dream led the WNBA in points in the paint. Kiah Stokes has been phenomenal at protecting the rim; on Monday, she joined Brittney Griner as the only players in league history to record at least four blocks in back-to-back finals games. That forces Atlanta out into floater range, which is a less efficient part of the floor, and the road team shot 3 of 14 on short mid-rangers.

If it weren't for their ability to get to the line and to force turnovers, the Dream would hardly be able to score in this series. They shot 7 of 11 in transition and 14 of 51 in the half court.

Perhaps some of this is mental. Smesko suggested that some players might be rushing their shots because of the defensive intensity. Hard close outs make jumpers more difficult. The stage of the finals causes some extra jitters, particularly for two franchises seeking their first title. This has been the longest season in WNBA history, and the wear could finally be setting in.

Smesko was mostly happy with Atlanta's shot quality for the second straight game, banking on his shooters to progress to the mean as the series continues. The Dream also enjoyed a dominant performance from Angel Reese, who seemed to be playing in a different offensive environment entirely with her 30 points on 10 of 16 shooting. Nakase had a similar sentiment, provided Golden State holds on to the ball long enough to take more field goals. Assuming full health for Williams and Tiffany Hayes, both of whom appear to have been banged up in the first two games, Nakase likes the shots her team is taking.

"I actually thought (Williams') looks were the same as usual, she just missed," Nakase said. "I wish I could say she's going to shoot 100 percent every night. That just isn't the case, and that's why, again for us, we do rely on our defense."

Both teams would settle for a lot less than 100 percent based on the tenor of this series so far. Even if it's by design, these games have been slugfests and more challenging on offense than any of the previous data would suggest.

With only one day off, which will be a travel day, before Game 3 in Atlanta, it's hard to imagine this getting too much better unless the sight lines in State Farm Arena are dramatically different. Never has the adage "defense wins championships" been tested to this extent.

articles.title: Grizzlies' strengths, weaknesses ahead of 2026-27 NBA season, including Cam Boozer
articles.summary: The Memphis Grizzlies enter the 2026-27 NBA season with a young team that features quality but unproven talent.
articles.body:
To call the Memphis Grizzlies a wild card for the 2026-27 NBA season might be an understatement.

Memphis revamped its roster, with many of the players who were among the team's longest-tenured veterans at the start of last season now gone. A new-look roster featuring only three players with more than four years of NBA experience will be tasked with showing improvement after the Grizzlies finished 25-57 last season.

Tuomas Iisalo is also relatively new to his role, entering his second full season as coach. This roster should be better equipped to execute his system after injuries and depth issues limited Memphis last season.

The Grizzlies open the season against the Utah Jazz on Oct. 21 (7 p.m. CT, DAZN-MEM) at FedExForum, beginning an 82-game journey expected to feature plenty of unpredictability.

The roster changes make it difficult to project what Memphis will look like over the course of the season. However, the preseason and flashes from last season have offered some clues about the team's potential strengths and weaknesses.

Memphis Grizzlies 2026-27 roster with free agency additions, losses

Potential strengths: Rebounding, 3-point shooting, depth

Grizzlies wing Cedric Coward answered confidently when asked whether a starting trio of himself, center Zach Edey and rookie forward Cam Boozer could rank among the NBA's best rebounding groups.

Coward and Edey have shown encouraging signs on the glass early in their careers, while Boozer enters the NBA with expectations of making an immediate impact as a rebounder. If all three deliver, Memphis could establish a physical identity built around controlling the boards.

The Grizzlies also have the potential to improve their 3-point shooting. Shooting woes plagued Memphis during its previous era, when Desmond Bane was often the only player in the starting lineup who consistently commanded respect from the 3-point line.

Ty Jerome, Scotty Pippen Jr., Cam Spencer, Olivier-Maxence Prosper, Quinten Post, Jerami Grant and Javon Small have all recorded NBA seasons in which they shot better than 40% from 3-point range. Coward, Jaylen Wells and GG Jackson are among the other potential rotation players capable of shooting at or above the league average.

Depth was another concern last season, when Iisalo faced criticism for relying on a deep rotation that struggled to produce consistent results. Memphis now has the potential to build a more productive second unit featuring veterans such as Grant and Isaiah Stewart alongside Jackson, Pippen and Spencer. Several players in that group have starting experience, giving Iisalo options as he experiments with lineups.

Potential weaknesses: Shot creation, youth, perimeter defense

One of Memphis' biggest challenges will be replacing the shot creation it lost after trading Ja Morant and Jaren Jackson Jr. Morant wasn't always an efficient isolation scorer, but he repeatedly showed an ability to create opportunities for himself in critical moments. Jackson also developed into a reliable option when the Grizzlies needed individual scoring.

Replacing that production won't be easy. Memphis will need multiple players to help fill the void. This issue could potentially show up late in games when most teams rely on their best scorers to hunt mismatches.

Youth is a factor in that equation. Boozer, Coward and GG Jackson could emerge as players capable of taking on larger scoring responsibilities in crucial moments. Jerome could also become a go-to option. However, the Grizzlies have limited experience among their potential closers. Jackson is 21 and entering his fourth season, Boozer is 19 and Coward is 23 entering his second season. Inexperience makes it difficult to predict who will step up when games are on the line.

Perimeter defense is another concern. Memphis kept Kris Murray after he entered training camp as a long shot to make the roster. His defensive ability helped strengthen his case.

Pippen and Wells should provide quality perimeter defense, but the Grizzlies lack proven depth in that area. Memphis will be counting on players such as Jackson and Coward to make strides defensively as they take on larger roles.

Key transaction to watch: The NBA trade deadline

Projecting where Memphis will finish is difficult, in part because the Grizzlies could become sellers at the NBA trade deadline if they fall out of the postseason picture.

Jerome and Grant could attract interest from contending teams seeking reinforcements for a playoff run. Both could become valuable veteran trade assets if Memphis decides to prioritize its long-term future over a push for the NBA playoffs.

How the Grizzlies approach the trade deadline will depend largely on their performance over the first half of the season. If the young roster develops quickly and Memphis remains competitive, the team could stay the course. If the growing pains prove too significant, the Grizzlies may have to consider whether moving veteran pieces would better serve their long-term goals.

Damichael Cole is the Memphis Grizzlies beat writer for The Commercial Appeal. Contact Damichael at damichael.cole@commercialappeal.com. Follow Damichael on X, formerly known as Twitter, @DamichaelC.
